posts.title: The Boundary That Helps Us Make Peace with What Is
posts.description: Since Thanksgiving 2022, I will always take the opportunity to share a holiday boundary we don’t talk about enough: Make room for grief. Because when you make space for your grief during the holidays, you are also making space for your humanity. You are choosing not to let the expectations of the season override what is true for you. That is a form of boundary-setting too. I learned this in the hardest way possible, as life often delivers wisdom through our wounds. My younger daughter doesn’t have any memories from Thanksgiving 2021. Our family was in the midst of a crisis, and for the first time, the four of us were not together on Thanksgiving. When the holiday came around again the following year, I knew better than to expect things to be as they once were. Making space for grief that year allowed us to meet each other where we were , rather than where we thought we “should” be. posts.title: When Criticism Has Kept the Best Parts of You Waiting
posts.description: Today, I’m sharing what became of something that began right here on Hands Free Mama thirteen years ago, when a teenager responded to one of my essays. I had no idea then how much our exchange would shape my life, or how it would eventually lead me to something I’ve spent nearly a year creating. I was two years into my writing career when a teenager left an unforgettable comment on one of my blog posts. “I’m in my late teens, and I’m sitting here with tears running down my face. I’m not a mom, but I have one. And she doesn’t know me. I know for a fact that she dislikes or downright hates many things that I like, feel, or believe, so I lie to her almost constantly. I’ve grown resigned to the fact that I will never have a relationship like I want with my mom (or dad, for that matter), and then something like this comes along and rips the feelings open all over again, making me question. posts.title: The People We Love Keep Becoming: How to Stay Curious
posts.description: Every September, I think about an index card I filled during Parent Night at my daughter’s middle school. “Connecting with each student is very important to me,” Mr. B explained. “I want to know what makes them excited… what makes them come alive.” As he continued speaking, it became clear that knowing his students wasn’t an extra part of teaching to him. It was the foundation of it. He told us that school had once felt like a prison to him. He knew what it was like to walk through the hallways with a desolate look on his face, believing no one noticed or cared enough to ask why. Mr. B wanted something different for the students who entered his classroom. By the time the intercom sounded, I had filled every inch of the index card with details about my child. I looked down at it and felt tears spring to my eyes. The teacher had asked about my girl. And more importantly, he wanted to know her. At the time, I thought I was giving Avery’s teacher information he could use that school year.
